# Amazon DynamoDB: questions

## Worked examples

<!-- quiz:start id=dynamodb-q021 -->
### Question 1

A company runs applications in private subnets of a VPC and servers in its on-premises data center. The data center connects to the VPC through AWS Direct Connect. Both the applications and the servers read and write items in an Amazon DynamoDB table in the same Region. The applications exchange several terabytes of data with DynamoDB each day; the servers exchange much less. All traffic to DynamoDB must reach the service privately, without using the public internet. Which TWO actions will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way? (Select TWO.)

- Create a NAT gateway in each Availability Zone, and route the DynamoDB traffic of the private subnets through the NAT gateways.
- Create a gateway endpoint for DynamoDB, and add the endpoint to the route tables of the private subnets of the applications.
- Route the requests of the data center servers over Direct Connect to the gateway endpoint that the private subnets use.
- Create an interface endpoint for DynamoDB in the VPC, and send the requests of the data center servers to it over Direct Connect.
- Create an interface endpoint for DynamoDB in the VPC, and send the requests of both the applications and the data center servers to it.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.**

- Create a gateway endpoint for DynamoDB, and add the endpoint to the route tables of the private subnets of the applications.
- Create an interface endpoint for DynamoDB in the VPC, and send the requests of the data center servers to it over Direct Connect.

**Deciding phrases.** "private subnets of a VPC", "servers in its on-premises data center", "without using the public internet", "MOST cost-effective"

**Think aloud.**

1. I read the last sentence first: it asks for two actions that keep all DynamoDB traffic private at the lowest cost.
2. I mark the constraints: applications in private subnets that move terabytes each day, servers in the data center behind Direct Connect, no public internet, and MOST cost-effectively.
3. Before I look at the options, I predict one interface endpoint for DynamoDB for everything, because PrivateLink serves both the VPC and the data center through private IP addresses.
4. I remove the NAT gateways, because a gateway endpoint reaches DynamoDB without a NAT device and NAT gateways charge for every gigabyte. I remove the data center route to the gateway endpoint, because gateway endpoints do not allow access from on-premises networks.
5. Between one interface endpoint for all callers and a gateway endpoint plus an interface endpoint, the difference is cost. My first idea breaks because the applications in the VPC can use a gateway endpoint at no additional charge, and PrivateLink is available for an additional cost.
6. Check: the gateway endpoint serves the applications at no extra charge, the interface endpoint serves the data center servers, and no request uses the public internet. Time: 90 seconds.

**Why.** The two groups of callers need two endpoint types. In the VPC, a gateway endpoint has [no additional charge for using gateway endpoints](../facts/vpc-endpoints.md#vpc-endpoints-wp-gateway-endpoint-no-additional-charge). Gateway endpoints do not serve the data center, so [you must use AWS PrivateLink](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-faq-gateway-endpoint-limits-use-privatelink), which reaches DynamoDB through [interface VPC endpoints and private IP addresses](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-faq-privatelink-interface-endpoints).

- A gateway endpoint reaches DynamoDB [without requiring an internet gateway or NAT device](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-faq-gateway-endpoint-no-igw-nat), and there is [no additional charge for using gateway endpoints](../facts/vpc-endpoints.md#vpc-endpoints-wp-gateway-endpoint-no-additional-charge).
- For on-premises access [you must use AWS PrivateLink](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-faq-gateway-endpoint-limits-use-privatelink), which uses [interface VPC endpoints and private IP addresses](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-faq-privatelink-interface-endpoints).

**Why not.**

- "Create a NAT gateway in each Availability Zone, ...": A gateway endpoint reaches DynamoDB [without requiring an internet gateway or NAT device](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-faq-gateway-endpoint-no-igw-nat), and NAT gateways charge per gigabyte [regardless of the traffic's source or destination](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-data-processing-any-destination).
- "Route the requests of the data center servers ...": Gateway endpoints do not allow access from on-premises networks; for that case [you must use AWS PrivateLink](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-faq-gateway-endpoint-limits-use-privatelink).
- "Create an interface endpoint for DynamoDB in the ...": This works, but PrivateLink is [available for an additional cost](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-faq-gateway-vs-privatelink-cost-note), and the daily terabytes of the applications can use a gateway endpoint without that cost.

**Twin.** If the stem said "only the applications in the VPC use the table" instead: the gateway endpoint alone, because there is [no additional charge for using gateway endpoints](../facts/vpc-endpoints.md#vpc-endpoints-wp-gateway-endpoint-no-additional-charge).

**Takeaway.** VPC callers use the gateway endpoint at no extra charge; data center callers use an interface endpoint.

**Review.** [IAM controls access and every table is encrypted at rest](2-deep.md#iam-controls-access-and-every-table-is-encrypted-at-rest-3-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 2

A company runs a voting application on an Amazon DynamoDB table in provisioned capacity mode. The table holds one item for each contest, and the contest ID is the only key attribute. Each vote adds 1 to a counter attribute of that item with an UpdateItem call, and the item is smaller than 1 KB. The application reads the total of each contest every second to show it on screen. During a televised final, almost every vote is for one contest, at about 4,000 votes each second. Amazon CloudWatch shows that consumed write capacity is far below the provisioned write capacity, but many vote updates are throttled. Which solution will BEST resolve the throttling?

- Raise the provisioned write capacity of the table to several times the current peak, and keep one counter item for each contest in the table.
- Switch the table to on-demand capacity mode so that DynamoDB adds capacity during the burst, and keep one counter item for each contest in the table.
- Write each vote as a new item with a unique vote ID as the key, and compute the total of each contest with a Scan that filters on the contest ID.
- Keep several counter items for each contest, with a random suffix from a fixed range added to the contest ID, and add up the counters for the total.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Keep several counter items for each contest, with a random suffix from a fixed range added to the contest ID, and add up the counters for the total.

**Deciding phrases.** "one item for each contest", "almost every vote is for one contest", "far below the provisioned write capacity", "BEST"

**Think aloud.**

1. I read the last sentence first: it asks for the solution that BEST resolves the throttling of the vote updates.
2. I mark the constraints: one counter item for each contest, about 4,000 small updates each second on one item, consumed write capacity far below the provisioned capacity, and a total that the screen reads every second.
3. Before I look at the options, I predict write sharding, because throttling with spare table capacity points to one hot item, and the hash of one key decides one partition.
4. I remove the higher provisioned capacity, because the table already has spare capacity and each partition has its own ceiling. I remove on-demand mode, because the hot item stays in one partition with the same ceiling.
5. Between one item for each vote with a Scan and several counters with random suffixes, the difference is how the total is read; the stem says the screen reads the total every second, so a Scan of every vote each second is the weaker design.
6. Check: random suffixes spread the updates over several counter items, the total adds a few counters, and every constraint is met. Time: 90 seconds.

**Why.** Consumed capacity is far below provisioned capacity, so the table is not short of capacity; one item is. A hash of its key [determines the partition](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-partition-key-hash-decides-partition), and a partition delivers at most [1,000 write units per second](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-partition-max-throughput). Write sharding is to [add a random number](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-write-sharding-random-suffix) to the key, and the total then needs to [query the items for all the suffixes](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-write-sharding-read-merge) and add them up.

**Why not.**

- "Raise the provisioned write capacity of the table ...": The table already has spare capacity; the limit is the partition of the hot item, which delivers at most [1,000 write units per second](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-partition-max-throughput).
- "Switch the table to on-demand capacity mode so ...": Every partition keeps its ceiling of [1,000 write units per second](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-partition-max-throughput) in either mode, and the hash of one key [determines the partition](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-partition-key-hash-decides-partition) of the hot item.
- "Write each vote as a new item with ...": It stops the throttling, but a Scan [reads every item in a table](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-scan-reads-every-item), so each total on screen reads every vote of every contest.

**Twin.** If the stem said "consumed write capacity equals the provisioned write capacity, and the votes are spread across many contests" instead: raise the provisioned write capacity, because the whole table is short of capacity.

**Takeaway.** Throttling on one item while the table has spare capacity means a hot key: shard it with a random suffix.

**Review.** [A hash of the partition key picks the partition so hot keys throttle](2-deep.md#a-hash-of-the-partition-key-picks-the-partition-so-hot-keys-throttle-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 3

An online store uses Amazon DynamoDB for its orders table. The partition key of the table is CustomerId, and the sort key is OrderDate. A new screen in the application must list the orders of one customer sorted by OrderTotal. The table currently holds two years of orders, and eventually consistent reads are acceptable. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Add a global secondary index with CustomerId as the partition key and OrderTotal as the sort key, and query the index for the screen.
- Define a local secondary index on the table with OrderTotal as the sort key, and query the index for the screen.
- Scan the table with a filter expression on CustomerId for each request, and sort the returned orders by OrderTotal in the application.
- Copy each order into a second table keyed by CustomerId and OrderTotal through a Lambda function that reads the stream of the table.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Add a global secondary index with CustomerId as the partition key and OrderTotal as the sort key, and query the index for the screen.

**Deciding phrases.** "currently holds two years of orders", "eventually consistent reads are acceptable", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** The new query keeps CustomerId as the partition key but needs another sort key, and the table already holds data. You can [add a new global secondary index](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-index-online-operations-gsi-vs-lsi) at any time, and its [index key schema can be different](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-gsi-key-schema-can-differ) from the table. Queries on it [support eventual consistency only](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-index-read-consistency-gsi-vs-lsi), which the screen accepts.

**Why not.**

- "Define a local secondary index on the table ...": The table already holds orders, and you [cannot add a local secondary index](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-index-online-operations-gsi-vs-lsi) to an existing table.
- "Scan the table with a filter expression on ...": It works, but a Scan [consumes the same amount of read capacity](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-scan-filter-same-read-capacity) with or without a filter, so each screen reads every order.
- "Copy each order into a second table keyed ...": It works, but the team writes and runs a function and a second table, while [DynamoDB maintains indexes automatically](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-indexes-maintained-automatically).

**Twin.** If the stem said "The table is being created now, and the new screen must use strongly consistent reads." instead: a local secondary index, because it is [created when the table is created](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-lsi-created-with-table).

**Takeaway.** For a new query on a table that already holds data, add a global secondary index.

**Review.** [Secondary indexes give the same items a second key to query](2-deep.md#secondary-indexes-give-the-same-items-a-second-key-to-query-5-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 4

A gaming company stores player profiles in an Amazon DynamoDB table. The game reads the same small set of profile items thousands of times each second, and every read is eventually consistent. Reads take a few milliseconds today, and the company wants them to return in microseconds. The company accepts minimal code changes, but it wants no new caching logic in the application. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST development effort?

- Create an Amazon ElastiCache cluster, and add code that reads each profile from the cache first and writes it to the cache after a miss.
- Raise the provisioned read capacity of the table to twice the current peak so that each profile read has more capacity to use.
- Create a DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) cluster for the table, and replace the DynamoDB client in the game with the DAX client.
- Move the player profiles into an Amazon ElastiCache cluster, and delete the DynamoDB table so that every read comes from memory.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create a DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) cluster for the table, and replace the DynamoDB client in the game with the DAX client.

**Deciding phrases.** "same small set of profile items", "return in microseconds", "no new caching logic", "LEAST development effort"

**Why.** The reads repeat, are eventually consistent and need microseconds, which is the DAX pattern. DAX fits applications that [read a small number of items more frequently](../facts/dax.md#dax-ideal-fastest-reads-hot-keys) than others. It is [API-compatible with DynamoDB](../facts/dax.md#dax-api-compatible-minimal-changes), so the game keeps its data access calls and swaps the client.

**Why not.**

- "Create an Amazon ElastiCache cluster, and add code ...": It works, but it adds the cache-aside logic that the company wants to avoid, while DAX needs [only minimal functional changes](../facts/dax.md#dax-api-compatible-minimal-changes) for the same reads.
- "Raise the provisioned read capacity of the table ...": Capacity sets how many reads the table accepts, not how fast each one returns, and DynamoDB alone gives [single-digit millisecond performance](../facts/dax.md#dax-modest-needs-use-dynamodb-alone).
- "Move the player profiles into an Amazon ElastiCache ...": ElastiCache is an [ephemeral cache for frequently accessed data](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-decision-guide-elasticache-caching-layer), so with the table deleted, the profiles lose their durable store.

**Twin.** If the stem said "every profile read must be strongly consistent" instead: DAX does not help, because [DAX passes strongly consistent read requests to DynamoDB](../facts/dax.md#dax-passes-through-strong-reads-and-transactions).

**Takeaway.** Repeated eventually consistent DynamoDB reads that need microseconds: add DAX and swap the client.

**Review.** [DAX answers repeated eventually consistent reads from memory in microseconds](2-deep.md#dax-answers-repeated-eventually-consistent-reads-from-memory-in-microseconds-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 5

A company stores product items in an Amazon DynamoDB table in provisioned capacity mode. Every item is 6 KB in size. The application needs to make 100 strongly consistent reads per second and 50 writes per second on these items. None of the writes are part of a transaction. A solutions architect needs to set the provisioned capacity of the table to match this load. How many read capacity units (RCUs) and write capacity units (WCUs) does the table need?

- 100 RCUs and 300 WCUs
- 200 RCUs and 50 WCUs
- 150 RCUs and 300 WCUs
- 200 RCUs and 300 WCUs

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** 200 RCUs and 300 WCUs

**Deciding phrases.** "6 KB in size", "100 strongly consistent reads per second", "50 writes per second"

**Why.** For reads, you [divide the item size of the operation by 4 KB](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-read-capacity-formula) and round up, so each strongly consistent read takes two units. For writes, you [divide the item size of the operation by 1 KB](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-write-capacity-formula), so each write takes six units. Multiply each by the request rates in the stem.

**Why not.**

- "100 RCUs and 300 WCUs": This prices each read like an eventually consistent read, but a unit gives [one strongly consistent read operation per second](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-rcu-definition) per block, so these reads need twice as many units.
- "200 RCUs and 50 WCUs": This counts one unit per write, but a unit covers [one write per second for an item up to 1 KB](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-wcu-definition), so a larger item takes more units.
- "150 RCUs and 300 WCUs": This divides the item size by the read block without rounding up, but sizes round up to the [next 4 KB multiple](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-read-rounding-4kb) before the division.

**Twin.** If the stem said "100 eventually consistent reads per second" instead: half the read units, because one RCU gives [two eventually consistent read operations per second](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-rcu-definition).

**Takeaway.** Reads round up to the [next 4 KB multiple](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-read-rounding-4kb) and writes to the [next 1 KB multiple](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-write-rounding-1kb); then multiply by the rate.

**Review.** [Read and write units depend on item size and read consistency](2-deep.md#read-and-write-units-depend-on-item-size-and-read-consistency-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 6

A company stores the order data of its online store in an Amazon DynamoDB table. The table uses provisioned capacity mode with auto scaling. Traffic is unpredictable: the table sits idle for hours, then spikes to earlier peak levels within minutes. The company wants to keep requests from being throttled and wants to lower the monthly cost of the table. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?

- Change the table to on-demand capacity mode, so that DynamoDB bills each read and write request that the application makes.
- Keep provisioned capacity mode with auto scaling, and purchase reserved capacity for the base level of reads and writes of the table.
- Keep provisioned capacity mode with auto scaling, and add a DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) cluster in front of the table for all requests.
- Keep provisioned capacity mode, turn off auto scaling, and set the read and write capacity to the highest level that the table has used.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Change the table to on-demand capacity mode, so that DynamoDB bills each read and write request that the application makes.

**Deciding phrases.** "Traffic is unpredictable", "the table sits idle for hours", "MOST cost-effective"

**Why.** For traffic that is idle for hours and then spikes, [on-demand capacity mode is the better choice](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-ondemand-better-for-fluctuating-traffic). The table is [billed per read or write request](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-ondemand-billed-per-request-zero-traffic-free), so the idle hours cost no throughput. In provisioned mode, auto scaling [does not respond instantly](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-throttling-with-autoscaling-possible) to a sudden spike.

**Why not.**

- "Keep provisioned capacity mode with auto scaling, and ...": Reserved capacity lowers the base price, but auto scaling [does not respond instantly](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-throttling-with-autoscaling-possible), so sudden spikes are still throttled.
- "Keep provisioned capacity mode with auto scaling, and ...": With DAX, data is [first written to the DynamoDB table](../facts/dax.md#dax-write-through-both-table-and-dax), so the cluster adds cost and the write spikes still reach the table.
- "Keep provisioned capacity mode, turn off auto scaling, ...": Capacity at the peak stops the throttling, but the company pays for the [hourly read and write capacity you have provisioned](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-provisioned-billing-basis) in every idle hour.

**Twin.** If the stem said "Traffic is steady-state and predictable: the table uses almost all of its provisioned capacity around the clock." instead: provisioned mode with reserved capacity, because it fits a [more steady and predictable usage pattern](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-provisioned-ideal-steady-predictable-usage).

**Takeaway.** Spiky, unpredictable DynamoDB traffic with idle hours: on-demand capacity mode, billed per request.

**Review.** [On-demand mode bills each request and needs no capacity plan](2-deep.md#on-demand-mode-bills-each-request-and-needs-no-capacity-plan-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=dynamodb-q009 -->
### Question 7

A company stores customer orders in an Amazon DynamoDB table. Point-in-time recovery is turned on with its default settings, and an on-demand backup of the table is taken every Sunday. The table also has a DynamoDB stream that a search service reads. On Tuesday at 14:05, a faulty release deleted thousands of order items. The team found the problem on Friday. The company must get the deleted items back as they were at 14:04, a point in time before the error. What should a solutions architect do?

- Restore the table to Tuesday at 14:04 directly into the existing table, so that the production table rolls back in place.
- Restore the Sunday on-demand backup to a new table, and copy the deleted items from the new table into the production table.
- Read the old images of the deleted items from the DynamoDB stream of the table, and write the items back into the production table.
- Restore the table to Tuesday at 14:04 as a new table, and copy the deleted items from the new table into the production table.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Restore the table to Tuesday at 14:04 as a new table, and copy the deleted items from the new table into the production table.

**Deciding phrases.** "as they were at 14:04", "The team found the problem on Friday"

**Why.** Point-in-time recovery protects a table [from accidental write or delete operations](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-pitr-protects-accidental-writes-deletes). The process [always restores to a new table](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-pitr-restores-to-new-table), because you [can't overwrite an existing table](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-restore-cannot-overwrite-existing-table) during a restore. The team restores to 14:04 and copies the deleted items back into production.

**Why not.**

- "Restore the table to Tuesday at 14:04 directly ...": You [can't overwrite an existing table](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-restore-cannot-overwrite-existing-table) during a restore, so no restore rolls the production table back in place.
- "Restore the Sunday on-demand backup to a new ...": The Sunday backup misses the orders that were created or changed between Sunday and Tuesday, so the items do not come back as they were at 14:04.
- "Read the old images of the deleted items ...": Stream records have a [lifetime of 24 hours](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-stream-records-24-hours), so the records of the Tuesday deletes were removed from the stream before Friday.

**Twin.** If the stem said "a faulty release deleted the whole table" instead: restore the [system backup](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-pitr-deleted-table-system-backup) that DynamoDB creates when a table with point-in-time recovery is deleted.

**Takeaway.** A DynamoDB point-in-time restore creates a new table; copy the items back or switch the application to it.

**Review.** [Every restore from a backup or a point in time creates a new table](2-deep.md#every-restore-from-a-backup-or-a-point-in-time-creates-a-new-table-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 8

A startup with a small team is building a serverless backend for a mobile app. AWS Lambda functions handle every request. Each request reads or writes one user session by its session ID, and no request joins session data with other data. Traffic swings from almost nothing at night to millions of requests at peak. Session data must be stored durably. Which database solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL in a Multi-AZ deployment, with each Lambda invocation opening its own database connection
- Amazon DynamoDB in on-demand capacity mode, with the session ID as the partition key of the session table
- A self-managed NoSQL database on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group across three Availability Zones
- A node-based Amazon ElastiCache for Memcached cluster as the only store of session data, keyed by session ID

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Amazon DynamoDB in on-demand capacity mode, with the session ID as the partition key of the session table

**Deciding phrases.** "reads or writes one user session by its session ID", "Session data must be stored durably", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** Each request reads one item by its key, with no joins, which fits a key-value database for [session stores or shopping carts](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-decision-guide-key-value-session-store). With DynamoDB you [don't need to provision any servers](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-serverless-no-servers). Lambda calls it without connection pools, because [DynamoDB uses an HTTP API](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-ddb-http-api-no-connections).

**Why not.**

- "Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL in a Multi-AZ deployment, ...": Unlike RDS, [DynamoDB uses an HTTP API](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-ddb-http-api-no-connections); a connection per invocation at peak needs pooling, and the team still sizes DB instances.
- "A self-managed NoSQL database on Amazon EC2 instances ...": DynamoDB, instead of a self-hosted NoSQL database, [can reduce operational overhead](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-wa-managed-nosql-reduces-overhead); here the team patches and scales the instances.
- "A node-based Amazon ElastiCache for Memcached cluster as ...": Memcached [node-based clusters do not support replication](../facts/elasticache.md#elasticache-memcached-node-based-no-replication-data-loss), so a node failure [will always result in some data loss](../facts/elasticache.md#elasticache-memcached-node-based-no-replication-data-loss), which fails the need to store sessions durably.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the app joins sessions with orders in ad hoc SQL reports" instead: a relational database such as Amazon Aurora, because DynamoDB [doesn't support a JOIN operator](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-no-join-operator).

**Takeaway.** Key-value sessions, spiky traffic and a small team: DynamoDB in on-demand mode.

**Review.** [Choose it or not](1-fast.md#choose-it-or-not-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 9

An online store uses Amazon DynamoDB for its orders table. The partition key of the table is CustomerId, and the sort key is OrderDate. A new screen in the application must list the orders of one customer sorted by OrderTotal. The table is being created now, and the new screen must use strongly consistent reads. The table will grow to millions of orders, and the screen must stay fast as the table grows. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Add a global secondary index with CustomerId as the partition key and OrderTotal as the sort key, and query the index for the screen.
- Define a local secondary index on the table with OrderTotal as the sort key, and query the index for the screen.
- Scan the table with a filter expression on CustomerId for each request, and sort the returned orders by OrderTotal in the application.
- Copy each order into a second table keyed by CustomerId and OrderTotal through a Lambda function that reads the stream of the table.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Define a local secondary index on the table with OrderTotal as the sort key, and query the index for the screen.

**Deciding phrases.** "is being created now", "must use strongly consistent reads", "must stay fast as the table grows", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** The screen needs strong reads on another sort key of the same customer. A local secondary index has the [same partition key as the base table](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-lsi-same-partition-key) and its own sort key. Strongly consistent reads are [only supported on tables and local secondary indexes](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-strong-reads-only-tables-and-lsi), and the table is new, so the index can be defined now.

**Why not.**

- "Add a global secondary index with CustomerId as ...": The screen needs strongly consistent reads, but queries on a global secondary index [support eventual consistency only](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-index-read-consistency-gsi-vs-lsi).
- "Scan the table with a filter expression on ...": It needs no index, but a Scan [always scans the entire table or secondary index](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-scan-less-efficient-than-query), and it slows [as a table or index grows](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-scan-slows-as-table-grows), so the screen does not stay fast.
- "Copy each order into a second table keyed ...": The copy is written from the stream after each change, and [reads from GSIs and streams are eventually consistent](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-gsi-and-streams-reads-eventual), so the copy can miss the latest write.

**Twin.** If the stem said "The table currently holds two years of orders, and eventually consistent reads are acceptable." instead: a global secondary index, because you can [add a new global secondary index](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-index-online-operations-gsi-vs-lsi) later.

**Takeaway.** Strong reads on another sort key of a new table: define a local secondary index at creation.

**Review.** [Secondary indexes give the same items a second key to query](2-deep.md#secondary-indexes-give-the-same-items-a-second-key-to-query-5-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=dynamodb-q007 -->
### Question 10

A company stores the order data of its online store in an Amazon DynamoDB table. The table uses provisioned capacity mode with auto scaling. Traffic is steady-state and predictable: the table uses almost all of its provisioned capacity around the clock. The company wants to keep requests from being throttled and wants to lower the monthly cost of the table. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?

- Change the table to on-demand capacity mode, so that DynamoDB bills each read and write request that the application makes.
- Keep provisioned capacity mode with auto scaling, and purchase reserved capacity for the base level of reads and writes of the table.
- Keep provisioned capacity mode with auto scaling, and add a DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) cluster in front of the table for all requests.
- Keep provisioned capacity mode, turn off auto scaling, and set the read and write capacity to the highest level that the table has used.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Keep provisioned capacity mode with auto scaling, and purchase reserved capacity for the base level of reads and writes of the table.

**Deciding phrases.** "Traffic is steady-state and predictable", "almost all of its provisioned capacity", "MOST cost-effective"

**Why.** The table uses almost all of its provisioned capacity all day. An ideal workload for provisioned mode has a [more steady and predictable usage pattern](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-provisioned-ideal-steady-predictable-usage), and on-demand costs less when average utilization is [below 35%](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-ondemand-cheaper-below-35-percent-utilization) or has quiet periods. This table runs near full use all day, so reserved capacity lowers the rate of the base load.

**Why not.**

- "Change the table to on-demand capacity mode, so ...": At steady, high use, on-demand is not the cheaper mode: it costs less when the average utilization is [below 35%](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-ondemand-cheaper-below-35-percent-utilization).
- "Keep provisioned capacity mode with auto scaling, and ...": With DAX, data is [first written to the DynamoDB table](../facts/dax.md#dax-write-through-both-table-and-dax), so the cluster adds cost and every write still uses the capacity of the table.
- "Keep provisioned capacity mode, turn off auto scaling, ...": Fixed capacity at the peak pays the standard rate for the [hourly read and write capacity you have provisioned](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-provisioned-billing-basis), with no reserved discount.

**Twin.** If the stem said "Traffic is unpredictable: the table sits idle for hours, then spikes to earlier peak levels within minutes." instead: on-demand capacity mode, because it is [billed per read or write request](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-ondemand-billed-per-request-zero-traffic-free).

**Takeaway.** Steady, predictable DynamoDB traffic near the provisioned level: provisioned mode plus reserved capacity.

**Review.** [Provisioned mode bills the capacity you set and auto scaling follows within minutes](2-deep.md#provisioned-mode-bills-the-capacity-you-set-and-auto-scaling-follows-within-minutes-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

## Extended

<!-- quiz:start id=dynamodb-q014 -->
### Question 11

A company stores support tickets as items in an Amazon DynamoDB table. Agents update each ticket many times during its life. When the status of a ticket changes to CLOSED, the company must send a satisfaction survey email to the customer in near real-time. The solution must not send a second email when an agent edits a ticket that is already closed. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Turn on DynamoDB Streams, and have an AWS Lambda function read the stream records once a week and email every ticket that was closed that week.
- Run an AWS Lambda function every minute on an Amazon EventBridge schedule that scans the table for closed tickets and emails the ones not yet emailed.
- Turn on DynamoDB Streams with new and old item images, and add an AWS Lambda trigger that emails when the status changes to CLOSED.
- Turn on DynamoDB Streams, and run an application on Amazon EC2 instances that polls the stream of the table and sends the survey emails.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Turn on DynamoDB Streams with new and old item images, and add an AWS Lambda trigger that emails when the status changes to CLOSED.

**Deciding phrases.** "status of a ticket changes to CLOSED", "near real-time", "already closed", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** The email follows one item change. DynamoDB Streams records a [time-ordered sequence of every item-level change](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-streams-time-ordered-changes) in [near-real time](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-streams-time-ordered-changes), and a stream has a [native integration with AWS Lambda](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-faq-streams-lambda-triggers). The old image shows whether the ticket was already closed, so an edit of a closed ticket sends no second email.

**Why not.**

- "Turn on DynamoDB Streams, and have an AWS ...": Stream records have a [lifetime of 24 hours](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-stream-records-24-hours), so a weekly job misses most changes, and the emails are days late.
- "Run an AWS Lambda function every minute on ...": It works, but each run reads the whole table, because in a Scan [DynamoDB reads every item](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-scan-reads-every-item), and the code tracks the emails it sent.
- "Turn on DynamoDB Streams, and run an application ...": It can work, but the team runs, patches and scales instances, while a Lambda trigger needs no servers to manage.

**Twin.** If the stem said "an audit job must replay every status change of the last 7 days" instead: Kinesis Data Streams for DynamoDB, because it keeps records [up to 1 year](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-streams-vs-kds-retention).

**Takeaway.** Run code on each item change with a stream and a Lambda trigger; keep old images to compare.

**Review.** [DynamoDB Streams records each item change in order for 24 hours](2-deep.md#dynamodb-streams-records-each-item-change-in-order-for-24-hours-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=dynamodb-q020 -->
### Question 12

A company will open ticket sales for a large concert at a fixed time next week. The tickets are stored in a new Amazon DynamoDB table in on-demand capacity mode, and the table has served only light test traffic so far. At the opening minute, the company expects a peak of many times more requests than the table has ever served. The company has stringent requirements: no request can be throttled. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Before the sale, raise the warm throughput of the table to the expected peak so that the table can serve that rate at once.
- Keep the table in on-demand capacity mode without other changes, because on-demand capacity mode serves any number of requests the moment they arrive.
- Switch the table to provisioned capacity mode with auto scaling at a 70% target utilization, and let auto scaling add capacity during the sale.
- Run a load script in the days before the sale that sends test traffic which keeps doubling until the table has served the expected peak.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Before the sale, raise the warm throughput of the table to the expected peak so that the table can serve that rate at once.

**Deciding phrases.** "has served only light test traffic", "many times more requests", "no request can be throttled", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** The table has served only light traffic, and on-demand mode [instantly accommodates up to double the previous peak](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-on-demand-previous-peak-double). Warm throughput is what a table [can instantaneously support](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-warm-throughput-definition). Raising it before the sale, called [pre-warming](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-warm-throughput-prewarm-for-peak-events), prepares the table for the known peak with one change.

**Why not.**

- "Keep the table in on-demand capacity mode without ...": On-demand mode [instantly accommodates up to double the previous peak](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-on-demand-previous-peak-double); above that, [throttling can occur](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-on-demand-throttle-if-double-within-30-min), and this jump is far larger.
- "Switch the table to provisioned capacity mode with ...": Auto scaling [does not respond instantly](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-throttling-with-autoscaling-possible), so requests in the opening minute are throttled before the new capacity arrives.
- "Run a load script in the days before ...": It can work, because the table then has a higher previous peak, but the team runs load tests for days instead of changing one table setting.

**Twin.** If the stem said "a peak about the same as the busiest day the table has already served" instead: keep on-demand mode, because it [instantly accommodates up to double the previous peak](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-on-demand-previous-peak-double).

**Takeaway.** A known launch far above any earlier peak: pre-warm the table by raising its warm throughput.

**Review.** [On-demand mode bills each request and needs no capacity plan](2-deep.md#on-demand-mode-bills-each-request-and-needs-no-capacity-plan-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=dynamodb-q022 -->
### Question 13

A company runs a profile service for users around the world. The service stores user profiles in an Amazon DynamoDB table in us-east-1. Users in Europe and Asia report slow saves, because every write travels to us-east-1. Each write must be served in the user's own Region, and the service must stay highly available if one Region fails. Which solution provides the LOWEST latency for writes from every user?

- Convert the table into a global table, send every write to the replica table in us-east-1, and fail writes over to another Region in an outage.
- Migrate the profiles to an Amazon Aurora global database with a cluster in each user Region, and send each write to the cluster in that Region.
- Convert the table into a global table with replica tables in the Regions of the users, and have each Region write to its local replica table.
- Create DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) clusters in Europe and in Asia that cache the table and accept the profile writes of local users.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Convert the table into a global table with replica tables in the Regions of the users, and have each Region write to its local replica table.

**Deciding phrases.** "users around the world", "served in the user's own Region", "LOWEST latency"

**Why.** The deciding phrase is local writes in every Region. Global tables are a [multi-Region, and multi-active database](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-faq-global-tables-multi-active), so every replica table accepts writes near its users. If one Region fails, the others keep serving reads and writes, because a global table has [no primary Region](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-faq-global-tables-no-failover-needed).

**Why not.**

- "Convert the table into a global table, send ...": It keeps the slow writes: a global table has [no primary Region](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-faq-global-tables-no-failover-needed), yet every write from Europe and Asia still travels to us-east-1.
- "Migrate the profiles to an Amazon Aurora global ...": In an Aurora global database, [only the primary cluster performs write operations](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-vs-aurora-global-database-single-writer), so every write from Europe and Asia still travels to the primary cluster's Region.
- "Create DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) clusters in Europe and ...": A DAX cluster works only with [tables that are in the same Region](../facts/dax.md#dax-same-region-as-tables), so clusters in Europe and Asia cannot serve a table in us-east-1.

**Twin.** If the stem said "users in Europe and Asia only read profiles, and the data is relational" instead: an Aurora global database, with [up to 10 read-only secondary AWS Regions](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-vs-aurora-global-database-single-writer) for local reads.

**Takeaway.** Local writes in many Regions: a DynamoDB global table, where every replica table accepts writes.

**Review.** [In a global table every replica accepts reads and writes](2-deep.md#in-a-global-table-every-replica-accepts-reads-and-writes-5-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=dynamodb-q015 -->
### Question 14

A company runs a loyalty program that stores the points balance of each user as an item in an Amazon DynamoDB table. A transfer moves points from one user to another. The transfer is transactional: the debit of one item and the credit of the other item must both succeed or both fail, and the debit must fail if the balance is too low. Clients sometimes time out and send the same transfer request again. The company must ensure that no transfer is applied twice. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST development effort?

- Send one BatchWriteItem request that holds both balance changes, and send the same request again when the client times out.
- Send two UpdateItem requests that change the balances with atomic counters, and retry each request when the client times out.
- Send two conditional UpdateItem requests, store each request ID in a second table, and write code that reverses a failed transfer.
- Send one TransactWriteItems request with both updates, a condition on the balance, and a client request token for each transfer.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Send one TransactWriteItems request with both updates, a condition on the balance, and a client request token for each transfer.

**Deciding phrases.** "must both succeed or both fail", "send the same transfer request again", "LEAST development effort"

**Why.** One TransactWriteItems request makes both updates with a [guaranteed all-or-nothing result](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-transactwriteitems-all-or-nothing). A condition on the balance stops a debit that is too large, because [a conditional write succeeds](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-conditional-write-succeeds-only-if-condition) only if its condition is met. The client can [include a client token](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-transactwriteitems-idempotent-client-token) to make a retried request idempotent.

**Why not.**

- "Send one BatchWriteItem request that holds both balance ...": With BatchWriteItem, [only some of the actions](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-transactwriteitems-vs-batchwriteitem) might succeed, so a debit can be written without its credit.
- "Send two UpdateItem requests that change the balances ...": With atomic counters, [the updates are not idempotent](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-atomic-counter-not-idempotent): each retry moves the points again, and the two requests can succeed separately.
- "Send two conditional UpdateItem requests, store each request ...": This design can work, but the team writes and maintains rollback code and duplicate checks that a transaction already provides.

**Twin.** If the stem said "a client can repeat a request an hour later" instead: also store each request ID and check it in the transaction, because a client token is valid for [10 minutes](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-transaction-client-token-10-minutes).

**Takeaway.** Two items that change together, with safe retries: TransactWriteItems with conditions and a client token.

**Review.** [Conditional writes and transactions stop one write from overwriting another](2-deep.md#conditional-writes-and-transactions-stop-one-write-from-overwriting-another-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=dynamodb-q017 -->
### Question 15

A company is building a reporting service for its sales team. Every week, analysts write new ad hoc SQL queries that join orders, customers, and products, and the access patterns are not known in advance. The data is relational and changes all day as new orders arrive. The team has two developers and no database administrator. Which database solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL, with the orders, customers, and products in related tables that the analysts query with SQL
- Amazon DynamoDB, with one table for each entity and a global secondary index for each report that the analysts need
- Amazon ElastiCache, as the fully managed in-memory store that holds the orders, customers, and products for the reports
- PostgreSQL on Amazon EC2 instances that the developers install, patch, back up, and scale for the SQL queries of the analysts

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL, with the orders, customers, and products in related tables that the analysts query with SQL

**Deciding phrases.** "new ad hoc SQL queries that join orders, customers, and products", "the access patterns are not known in advance", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** The analysts write new joins every week, so the access patterns are not known in advance. The AWS decision guide points to Aurora for [less predictable query patterns](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-decision-guide-aurora-relational-joins). Aurora is a [fully managed relational database engine](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-is-managed-relational-engine), so the two developers do not run database instances themselves.

**Why not.**

- "Amazon DynamoDB, with one table for each entity ...": DynamoDB [doesn't support a JOIN operator](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-no-join-operator), and NoSQL data is [queried efficiently in a limited number of ways](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-nosql-queries-efficient-in-limited-ways), not by new ad hoc queries.
- "Amazon ElastiCache, as the fully managed in-memory store ...": ElastiCache is an [ephemeral cache for frequently accessed data](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-decision-guide-elasticache-caching-layer), a layer in front of a database, so it is not the store of record for the reports.
- "PostgreSQL on Amazon EC2 instances that the developers ...": PostgreSQL on EC2 runs the joins, but the two developers patch, back up, and scale the instances themselves.

**Twin.** If the stem said "every request reads one order by its order ID, with no joins" instead: Amazon DynamoDB, because for that access AWS says to [consider a NoSQL database such as DynamoDB](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-wa-oltp-dynamodb-vs-rds-joins).

**Takeaway.** Ad hoc SQL with joins and unknown access patterns: a relational engine such as Aurora, not DynamoDB.

**Review.** [Choose it or not](1-fast.md#choose-it-or-not-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=dynamodb-q019 -->
### Question 16

A web application stores user sessions in an Amazon DynamoDB table that holds millions of items. The application reads each session by its session ID. Each session must expire one hour after its last use, and the application must never accept an expired session. Old session items must be removed from the table automatically. Which TWO actions will meet these requirements in the MOST operationally efficient way? (Select TWO.)

- Store the expiry time of each session as a Number in Unix epoch seconds, and enable Time to Live on that attribute.
- Enable Time to Live on the expiry attribute, and accept every session item that a read returns, because expired items are gone.
- In every session read, compare the stored expiry time with the current time, and reject any session item that has expired.
- Store the expiry time of each session as an ISO 8601 date string, and enable Time to Live on that attribute.
- Run a Lambda function every minute on an Amazon EventBridge schedule that scans the table and deletes expired session items.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.**

- Store the expiry time of each session as a Number in Unix epoch seconds, and enable Time to Live on that attribute.
- In every session read, compare the stored expiry time with the current time, and reject any session item that has expired.

**Deciding phrases.** "must never accept an expired session", "removed from the table automatically", "MOST operationally efficient"

**Why.** TTL removes old sessions without code: the expiry is a Number in [Unix epoch time format at the seconds granularity](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-ttl-attribute-number-epoch-seconds), and the deletes run [without consuming any write throughput](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-faq-ttl-no-write-throughput). TTL is not exact: items go [within a few days of their expiration time](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-ttl-deletes-within-days-no-wcu), so every read also rejects an expired session.

- The TTL attribute uses [Unix epoch time format at the seconds granularity](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-ttl-attribute-number-epoch-seconds), and TTL deletes items [without consuming any write throughput](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-faq-ttl-no-write-throughput).
- Expired items [continue to show in read and write operations](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-ttl-expired-items-visible-until-deleted) until deletion, so the application checks the expiry time on every read.

**Why not.**

- "Enable Time to Live on the expiry attribute, ...": DynamoDB deletes expired items [within a few days of their expiration time](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-ttl-deletes-within-days-no-wcu), so a read can still return an expired session.
- "Store the expiry time of each session as ...": Items whose TTL attribute is not a Number are [ignored by the TTL process](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-ttl-non-number-attribute-ignored), so the sessions stay in the table.
- "Run a Lambda function every minute on an ...": The job works, but the team maintains code, and its scans and deletes use capacity; TTL deletes [without consuming any write throughput](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-faq-ttl-no-write-throughput).

**Twin.** If the stem said "an expired session can be accepted for a few days" instead: TTL alone is enough, because DynamoDB deletes items [within a few days of their expiration time](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-ttl-deletes-within-days-no-wcu).

**Takeaway.** TTL deletes expired items within days, not at once; reject expired items in every read.

**Review.** [Time to Live deletes expired items without using write capacity](2-deep.md#time-to-live-deletes-expired-items-without-using-write-capacity-3-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=dynamodb-q012 -->
### Question 17

A company runs its order service in us-east-1 and stores the orders in an Amazon DynamoDB table in on-demand capacity mode in the same Region. The company is planning cross-Region disaster recovery for a failure of the whole Region. If us-east-1 fails, users must keep reading and writing orders in us-west-2 immediately, with no restore step. Which solution meets these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?

- Convert the table into a global table, and add a replica table in us-west-2 that the application can read from and write to.
- Use AWS Backup to back up the table every hour, and copy each backup to a backup vault in us-west-2 for restores.
- Convert the table into a global table, and add replica tables in us-west-2 and in eu-west-1 that the application can read from and write to.
- Create a DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) cluster in us-west-2 that caches the items of the table and serves them to the application during an outage.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Convert the table into a global table, and add a replica table in us-west-2 that the application can read from and write to.

**Deciding phrases.** "keep reading and writing orders in us-west-2 immediately", "with no restore step", "MOST cost-effective"

**Why.** Users need to write in us-west-2 at once, with no restore step. A global table has [no primary Region](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-faq-global-tables-no-failover-needed), so no database failover is needed, and replication gives an [RPO of a few seconds](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-dr-global-tables-mrec-rto-zero). One replica table in us-west-2 meets the need at the lowest cost.

**Why not.**

- "Use AWS Backup to back up the table ...": A backup is restored into a new table before anyone can use it, and hourly copies give an [RPO of 1 hour](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-dr-aws-backup-rpo-1-hour), not writes in us-west-2 at once.
- "Convert the table into a global table, and ...": It works, but the eu-west-1 replica table adds a replicated write request unit (rWRU) charge, [one rWRU per replica table](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-gt-rwru-per-replica) for every write, which no requirement needs.
- "Create a DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) cluster in us-west-2 ...": A DAX cluster can work only with [tables that are in the same Region](../facts/dax.md#dax-same-region-as-tables), so a cluster in us-west-2 cannot serve this table.

**Twin.** If the stem said "If us-east-1 fails, a restore in us-west-2 within hours is acceptable, and so is losing up to 1 hour of data." instead: AWS Backup with hourly copies, for an [RPO of 1 hour](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-dr-aws-backup-rpo-1-hour).

**Takeaway.** Reads and writes in a second Region at once: a global table with one replica table there.

**Review.** [In a global table every replica accepts reads and writes](2-deep.md#in-a-global-table-every-replica-accepts-reads-and-writes-5-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=dynamodb-q013 -->
### Question 18

A company keeps 5 years of order history in an Amazon DynamoDB table that uses the DynamoDB Standard table class. The company must retain all of the orders, and the application reads old orders through the same DynamoDB API as new orders. Orders older than one month are infrequently accessed. Storage is about 70% of the monthly bill of the table. The company does not want to change the application code. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?

- Enable Time to Live on the order table so that DynamoDB deletes each order item one month after the order date.
- Export the orders older than one month to Amazon S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval, and delete those orders from the table.
- Change the table class of the order table from DynamoDB Standard to the DynamoDB Standard-Infrequent Access (DynamoDB Standard-IA) table class.
- Keep the DynamoDB Standard table class, and purchase reserved capacity for the reads and writes that the table uses each month.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Change the table class of the order table from DynamoDB Standard to the DynamoDB Standard-Infrequent Access (DynamoDB Standard-IA) table class.

**Deciding phrases.** "must retain all of the orders", "infrequently accessed", "Storage is about 70% of the monthly bill", "MOST cost-effective"

**Why.** Storage is about 70% of the bill, and DynamoDB Standard-IA suits tables whose storage is [approximately 50% or more of the overall monthly cost](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-table-class-standard-vs-ia-50-percent-storage). It offers the [same performance, durability, and availability](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-table-class-standard-ia-same-performance) as Standard, and the switch [does not require changing your application code](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-table-class-switch-no-code-change).

**Why not.**

- "Enable Time to Live on the order table ...": Deleting old orders lowers the bill, but it breaks the requirement to retain all of the orders.
- "Export the orders older than one month to ...": Archived orders leave the table, so the application can no longer read them through the same DynamoDB API.
- "Keep the DynamoDB Standard table class, and purchase ...": Reserved capacity discounts only reads and writes, but here [storage is the dominant cost](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-table-class-standard-ia-lower-storage-cost), and Standard-IA lowers it.

**Twin.** If the stem said "Storage is about 20% of the monthly bill" instead: keep DynamoDB Standard, which suits tables whose storage is [approximately 50% or less of the overall monthly cost](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-table-class-standard-vs-ia-50-percent-storage).

**Takeaway.** When storage is half or more of a DynamoDB bill, switch the table class to Standard-IA.

**Review.** [Time to Live deletes expired items without using write capacity](2-deep.md#time-to-live-deletes-expired-items-without-using-write-capacity-3-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->
